lists.title: Indonesian A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Indonesian: verbs that never conjugate, adjectives after the noun, tidak vs. bukan negation, possession by word order, plural reduplication, time markers before the verb, apakah questions, and the formal/inclusive pronoun splits.

lists.title: Indonesian A2 Grammar Path
lists.description: The affix system starts here: meN- active verbs and their nasal changes, ber- intransitives, the everyday di- passive, comparison, classifiers, ada, question words, modals, place prepositions, and the free-standing aspect markers.

lists.title: Indonesian B1 Grammar Path
lists.description: The suffixes that change what a verb points at — -kan and -i — plus peN- agent nouns, ke-...-an and per-...-an abstractions, the all-purpose yang, both passive types, purpose and conditional clauses, and the four jobs of se-.

lists.title: Indonesian B2 Grammar Path
lists.description: ter- for accidents and states, memper- causatives, reduplication beyond the plural, reported speech with bahwa, the discourse particles -lah/-kah/-pun, formal connectors, and the agentless passive that Indonesian prefers.

lists.title: Indonesian C1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Register: bahasa baku beside Jakarta speech, the noun-heavy style of official prose, and affix pairs on one root whose meanings no rule predicts.

lists.title: Indonesian C2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Switching register inside a single text, affixed words that have drifted from their roots, and the fronting and ellipsis of journalistic style.

points.title: Verbs don't conjugate
points.function: Use one verb form for every subject and tense
points.explanation: Indonesian verbs never change form for person, number, or tense — the same word mau means "want," "wants," and "wanted," no matter who's speaking or when. Saya mau, kamu mau, dia mau, kami mau — same verb every time. Tense and aspect are shown by separate marker words instead of by changing the verb itself.

drills.translation: I want to eat.
drills.hint: want — same form for every subject

drills.translation: We want to eat.
drills.hint: want — unchanged, no conjugation for "we"

drills.translation: He/she wants to eat.
drills.hint: want — unchanged, no -s ending like English

drills.translation: They don't drink coffee.
drills.hint: drink — one form serves every subject, in a negative sentence too

drills.translation: Did you go to the market yesterday?
drills.hint: go — there is no past form to reach for, even in a question about yesterday

drills.translation: My mother lives in Bandung.
drills.hint: live, reside — Indonesian has nothing like the English third-person ending

drills.sentence: Kemarin kami {{answer}} di rumah teman saya.
drills.translation: Yesterday we slept at my friend's house.
drills.hint: sleep — the plain verb covers a past event; only the time word says when

points.title: Adjectives follow the noun
points.function: Put adjectives in the right place
points.explanation: Indonesian adjectives come AFTER the noun they describe, the reverse of English: rumah besar, literally "house big," means "a big house," not "big house." Buku baru = "a new book," teman baik = "a good friend."

drills.translation: a big house
drills.hint: big — placed after the noun

drills.translation: a new book
drills.hint: new — after the noun, not before

drills.translation: a good friend
drills.hint: good — adjective follows the noun

drills.translation: He has a black cat.
drills.hint: a black cat — name the animal first, then its colour

drills.translation: This is my new friend.
drills.hint: new friend — the describing word sits between the noun and its owner

drills.translation: We eat at that small restaurant.
drills.hint: small — it follows the noun and comes before the word meaning 'that'

points.title: Negation: tidak vs. bukan
points.function: Pick the right word for "not"
points.explanation: Indonesian has two words for "not," and they aren't interchangeable: tidak negates verbs and adjectives (tidak besar = "not big"), while bukan negates nouns and identity (bukan guru = "not a teacher"). Using the wrong one is a classic learner mix-up.

drills.translation: This house isn't big.
drills.hint: not — negates the adjective besar

drills.translation: I don't like (it).
drills.hint: not — negates the verb suka

drills.translation: This isn't my book.
drills.hint: not — negates the noun/identity, not tidak

drills.translation: Why didn't you come yesterday?
drills.hint: not — the negator for a verb; the question word in front makes no difference

drills.translation: I'm not Japanese.
drills.hint: not — what follows names who someone is, a noun, so the verb negator is wrong here

drills.translation: He doesn't want to eat.
drills.hint: not — it goes in front of the verb it cancels, ahead of the word for 'want'

drills.translation: That car isn't mine.
drills.hint: not — 'punya saya' says whose it is, and identity like that takes the noun negator

points.title: Possession by word order
points.function: Show ownership with no possessive marker
points.explanation: To show possession, Indonesian just places the owner right after the noun — no word for "of" and no apostrophe-s needed: rumah saya, literally "house I," means "my house." Buku dia = "his/her book."

drills.translation: my house
drills.hint: my — just place the pronoun after the noun

drills.translation: his/her book
drills.hint: his/her — no possessive marker needed

drills.translation: our friend (yours and mine)
drills.hint: our — inclusive "we," right after the noun

drills.translation: What's your name?
drills.hint: your (one person, informal) — the owner word simply follows the thing owned, even in a question

drills.translation: This is my father's car.
drills.hint: my father, as the owner — an owner slot can itself be a noun with its own owner, in the same order

drills.translation: Their dog is very big.
drills.hint: their — no special possessive form exists; the plain pronoun sits right after the noun

points.title: Plural by reduplication
points.function: Make a noun plural by doubling it
points.explanation: Indonesian often shows plurality by doubling the whole word: buku ("book") → buku-buku ("books"); anak ("child") → anak-anak ("children"). Reduplication isn't required everywhere — a number or context already makes plurality clear — but it's the classic native way to say "many" of something.

drills.translation: There are books at home.
drills.hint: books — the plural repeats the singular whole, with a hyphen joining the two halves

drills.translation: There are children in the city.
drills.hint: children — no plural ending exists; the noun is doubled instead, the two halves joined by a hyphen

drills.translation: I have friends.
drills.hint: friends — the noun is spoken twice, hyphenated, to mean more than one (punya = 'to have')

drills.translation: Where are those people now?
drills.hint: people — this plural is made by repetition, not by an ending

drills.sentence: Saya suka {{answer}} tua di kota ini.
drills.translation: I like the old houses in this city.
drills.hint: houses — repeat the noun in full, and keep the describing word after it

drills.translation: On Sundays, the shops are closed.
drills.hint: shops — say the noun twice, hyphenated, for the plural

drills.translation: She doesn't like big cities.
drills.hint: cities — the doubled noun carries the plural; a negative sentence needs no other marking

points.title: Time markers before the verb: sudah, belum, akan
points.function: Show past, not-yet, and future without changing the verb
points.explanation: Indonesian shows time with a marker word placed BEFORE the verb, since the verb itself never changes: sudah ("already," for something done), belum ("not yet"), and akan ("will," for the future). Saya sudah makan = "I've already eaten"; Saya belum makan = "I haven't eaten yet"; Saya akan makan = "I will eat."

drills.translation: I have already eaten.
drills.hint: already — marks a completed action, before the verb

drills.translation: I haven't eaten yet.
drills.hint: not yet — before the verb

drills.translation: I will eat.
drills.hint: will — marks the future, before the verb

drills.translation: Have you taken your medicine yet?
drills.hint: already — the completion marker, in front of the verb in a question too

drills.translation: Tomorrow we will go to Bali.
drills.hint: will — the future marker still comes before the verb, even when a time word names the day

drills.translation: My child is grown up now.
drills.hint: already — the same completion marker works in front of a describing word, not only a verb

points.title: Yes/no questions with apakah
points.function: Ask a yes/no question without reordering the sentence
points.explanation: The easiest way to ask a yes/no question is to place apakah at the very front of the sentence — the word order after it doesn't change at all: Apakah kamu mau makan? ("Do you want to eat?"), literally "[question] you want eat?" In casual speech, apakah is often dropped and rising intonation alone signals the question.

drills.translation: Do you want to eat?
drills.hint: the yes/no question word that stands in front of the whole clause; nothing behind it moves

drills.translation: Does he/she like this book?
drills.hint: the question marker Indonesian puts at the very start — the statement order is kept intact after it

drills.translation: Is this your house?
drills.hint: the front-of-sentence marker that turns a statement into a yes/no question

drills.translation: Don't you like coffee?
drills.hint: the yes/no question word still leads, even when the sentence already carries a negative

drills.translation: Have they arrived yet?
drills.hint: open the question with the marker; the completed-action word stays in its usual place before the verb

drills.translation: Can we sit here?
drills.hint: front the yes/no question word — subject and verb behind it keep statement order

drills.translation: Do you have a moment? (formal)
drills.hint: the question opener expected in polite and written Indonesian, placed before the subject

points.title: Formal vs. informal "you"; inclusive vs. exclusive "we"
points.function: Choose the pronoun that matches the social situation
points.explanation: Indonesian pronouns encode social distinctions English doesn't: kamu is informal "you," while anda is the formal, polite version used with strangers or in writing. "We" also splits in two: kita includes the person you're talking to, kami excludes them — a difference English simply doesn't mark.

drills.translation: Would you like to eat? (formal/polite)
drills.hint: you, formal/polite — used with strangers or in writing

drills.translation: We (not you) are going home.
drills.hint: we, excluding the listener

drills.translation: We (including you) are going to the city.
drills.hint: we, including the listener

drills.translation: Where do you live now?
drills.hint: you — speaking to a friend of your own age; the polite written form would sound stiff here

drills.sentence: Silakan isi formulir ini sebelum {{answer}} masuk.
drills.translation: Please fill in this form before you enter.
drills.hint: you — the distant, respectful form a public notice uses for a reader it has never met

drills.translation: We have already eaten, but you haven't.
drills.hint: we — one side of the contrast, and the person addressed is on the other side

drills.translation: Come on, let's leave now!
drills.hint: we — an invitation gathers the listener in rather than leaving them out

points.title: The meN- prefix: active transitive verbs
points.function: Form active verbs and hear the nasal change
points.explanation: meN- is the standard active-verb prefix, and its nasal ADAPTS to the first sound of the root: b/p → mem- (baca → membaca, potong → memotong), d/t → men- (dengar → mendengar, tulis → menulis), g/k/vowel → meng- (ganggu → mengganggu, kirim → mengirim, ambil → mengambil), s → meny- (sewa → menyewa), and l/m/n/r/w/y → me- (lihat → melihat). With p, t, k, s the first letter usually DROPS: potong → memotong, not *mempotong. Dictionaries list the bare root, so recognising the pattern is how you look a word up.

drills.translation: I read a book every night.
drills.hint: baca + meN- → mem- before b

drills.translation: He writes a letter to his mother.
drills.hint: tulis + meN- → men-, and t drops

drills.translation: They sent that parcel yesterday.
drills.hint: kirim + meN- → meng-, and k drops

drills.translation: We watch a film at the cinema.
drills.hint: tonton + meN- → men-, t drops

drills.sentence: Apakah kamu {{answer}} kamar ini setiap bulan?
drills.translation: Do you rent this room every month?
drills.hint: sewa + meN- — the nasal form that goes with an s root, and the s itself drops out

drills.sentence: Saya belum {{answer}} rambut sejak bulan lalu.
drills.translation: I haven't cut my hair since last month.
drills.hint: potong + meN- — the same nasal as before b, but a p drops where the b of baca stays

drills.translation: From my bedroom window I see the sea.
drills.hint: lihat + meN- — before l the nasal vanishes and the root keeps every letter

points.title: The ber- prefix: intransitive and stative verbs
points.function: Say what someone does or has, with no object
points.explanation: ber- makes verbs that take no object — activities (berjalan 'walk', berenang 'swim', bekerja 'work'), states (berdiri 'stand'), and 'having' (beranak 'have children', berambut panjang 'have long hair'). Before a root starting with r, and in a few fixed words, it shortens to be-: ber + renang → berenang, ber + kerja → bekerja. Where meN- points AT something, ber- doesn't.

drills.translation: The children play in the park.
drills.hint: main + ber- — intransitive

drills.translation: My father works at the hospital.
drills.hint: kerja + ber- → be- (irregular)

drills.translation: We swim every Sunday.
drills.hint: renang + ber- → be- before r

drills.translation: She walks to school every morning.
drills.hint: jalan + ber-

drills.translation: My mother has short hair now.
drills.hint: rambut + ber- — the 'having' sense: the prefix on a noun says the subject possesses it

drills.sentence: Jangan {{answer}} terlalu cepat, saya tidak mengerti.
drills.translation: Don't speak too fast, I don't understand.
drills.hint: bicara + ber- — no object follows; the person you address arrives with dengan

points.title: The di- passive: putting the object first
points.function: Lead with what was affected, not who did it
points.explanation: Indonesian uses the passive far more than English. Swap meN- for di- and the object becomes the subject: Saya membaca buku itu → Buku itu dibaca (oleh saya). The agent is optional and marked with oleh. This is neutral, everyday word order — not the formal, evasive register English passive carries.

drills.translation: That book is read by thousands of people.
drills.hint: baca + di- — the object leads

drills.translation: This letter was sent yesterday.
drills.hint: kirim + di-

drills.translation: That house was sold last year.
drills.hint: jual + di-

drills.translation: The door was opened by the guard.
drills.hint: buka + di-

drills.translation: When was this building built?
drills.hint: bangun + di- — the thing affected is the subject and the builder is left unsaid

drills.translation: The back door wasn't locked last night.
drills.hint: kunci + di- — the door leads the sentence, so the verb takes the passive prefix, not meN-

drills.sentence: Kue ini {{answer}} oleh ibu saya setiap tahun.
drills.translation: This cake is made by my mother every year.
drills.hint: buat + di- — ordinary Indonesian, not stiff English; the maker follows oleh

points.title: Comparison: lebih, daripada, paling, ter-
points.function: Say more, less, and most
points.explanation: lebih X (daripada Y) is 'more X (than Y)': Dia lebih tinggi daripada saya. For the superlative you have two choices — paling X (paling besar) or the prefix ter- (terbesar); they mean the same, ter- is tighter and commoner in writing. 'Less' is kurang, and 'as … as' is se-: setinggi 'as tall as'.

drills.translation: He is taller than me.
drills.hint: the 'more' marker that sits in front of the adjective, paired with the 'than' word later in the sentence

drills.translation: This is the tastiest restaurant in town.
drills.hint: the free-standing superlative word placed before the adjective — the two-word alternative to the ter- prefix

drills.translation: That is the highest mountain in Indonesia.
drills.hint: ter- + tinggi

drills.translation: My sibling is as tall as me.
drills.hint: se- + adjective

drills.sentence: Naik kereta lebih cepat {{answer}} naik bus.
drills.translation: Taking the train is faster than taking the bus.
drills.hint: the word that introduces what something is measured against, after the adjective

points.title: Classifiers: orang, ekor, buah
points.function: Count things the way Indonesian counts them
points.explanation: A number doesn't attach straight to a noun in careful Indonesian — a classifier sits between: orang for people (tiga orang guru), ekor for animals (dua ekor kucing), buah for things (lima buah rumah). Everyday speech often drops buah, but orang and ekor are alive and expected.

drills.translation: There are three teachers here.
drills.hint: Teachers are people, so the classifier for humans goes between the number and the noun.

drills.translation: I have two cats.
drills.hint: Cats are animals; use the classifier reserved for creatures, not the one for people.

drills.translation: She bought five books.
drills.hint: Books are neither people nor animals, so the classifier for inanimate things belongs here.

drills.translation: Ten students came.
drills.hint: Students are people too, so the same human classifier follows the number.

drills.translation: How many people would you like to book a table for?
drills.hint: The count is of human beings, and here the classifier stands on its own with no noun after it.

drills.sentence: Kami melihat tiga {{answer}} burung di pohon itu.
drills.translation: We saw three birds in that tree.
drills.hint: Birds are animals, so the number takes the animal classifier before the noun.

drills.sentence: Kamu perlu berapa {{answer}} kursi untuk rapat besok?
drills.translation: How many chairs do you need for tomorrow's meeting?
drills.hint: Chairs are inanimate things, so the number takes the classifier used for objects.

points.title: ada: existence, having, and 'there is'
points.function: Say something exists or is present
points.explanation: ada covers 'there is/are', 'to be present', and informally 'to have': Ada masalah 'There's a problem', Dia ada di kantor 'He's at the office', Saya ada uang 'I have money' (punya is the careful word for owning). Negated it becomes tidak ada.

drills.translation: There is a problem with this computer.
drills.hint: Opens the sentence with bare existence: something is out there, and no subject is needed before it.

drills.translation: He is at the office now.
drills.hint: Says the person is physically present, with the place phrase following it.

drills.translation: There is nobody at home.
drills.hint: After tidak comes the existence verb; together they say nobody is there.

drills.translation: Any questions?
drills.hint: Existence again, this time opening a short question that invites the listener to speak up.

drills.translation: Do you have small change?
drills.hint: The everyday spoken way to ask whether someone has something on them; careful writing would use punya instead.

drills.translation: There is still a little milk in the fridge.
drills.hint: The existence word that says something is there, placed right after masih.

points.title: Question words
points.function: Ask what, who, where, when, why, how
points.explanation: apa 'what', siapa 'who', di mana 'where', ke mana 'where to', kapan 'when', mengapa/kenapa 'why', bagaimana 'how', berapa 'how much/many'. Unlike English they usually stay where the answer would go: Kamu tinggal di mana? not *Di mana kamu tinggal? (though fronting is fine and common too).

drills.translation: Where do you live?
drills.hint: The question word for place — Indonesian leaves it in the very slot the answer would fill, right after di.

drills.translation: What is your name?
drills.hint: Indonesian asks for a name with the person question word, not the one for things.

drills.translation: When are you coming?
drills.hint: The time question: on what day, at what hour.

drills.translation: How much is it?
drills.hint: Asking a quantity, here the amount of money something costs.

drills.translation: What are you reading?
drills.hint: The word for 'what', left in the object slot where the answer would go rather than moved to the front.

drills.translation: How do I get to the station?
drills.hint: The manner question, fronted here: it asks by what means or in what way.

drills.translation: Who are you going to the market with?
drills.hint: The person question word again, this time left in place after the preposition instead of moved to the front.

points.title: Modality: bisa, boleh, harus, mau
points.function: Say can, may, must, want
points.explanation: These sit straight before the verb, unchanged: bisa 'can, be able', boleh 'may, be allowed', harus 'must', mau/ingin 'want', perlu 'need'. Negate with tidak (tidak bisa) except boleh, where careful speech prefers tidak boleh for 'must not'.

drills.translation: I can speak Indonesian.
drills.hint: Ability, something you have learned to do; the modal goes straight before the verb and never changes shape.

drills.translation: You may come in now.
drills.hint: Granting permission rather than describing what someone is able to do.

drills.translation: We must go now.
drills.hint: Obligation with no choice about it, marked by a word before the verb.

drills.translation: He can't come today.
drills.hint: Negated ability: something prevents him, so tidak plus the modal of being able.

drills.translation: What would you like to drink?
drills.hint: Taking an order: the plain spoken verb of wanting rather than the more formal ingin, standing directly before the verb.

drills.translation: May I sit here?
drills.hint: Asking for permission rather than stating ability; the modal sits between the subject and the verb.

drills.sentence: Kamu tidak {{answer}} khawatir, saya sudah membeli tiketnya.
drills.translation: You don't need to worry, I've already bought the tickets.
drills.hint: Telling someone there is no need at all, which is not the same as lifting an obligation with harus.

points.title: Place prepositions: di, ke, dari
points.function: Say where something is, where it's going, where it came from
points.explanation: di 'at/in/on' (static), ke 'to' (motion toward), dari 'from' (origin). They combine with position nouns for detail: di atas meja 'on the table', di dalam kotak 'inside the box', di depan rumah 'in front of the house'. Keep di the preposition (written separate) apart from di- the passive prefix (written joined).

drills.translation: The book is on the table.
drills.hint: Nothing is moving, so the static preposition pairs with atas to name the surface.

drills.translation: I'm going to the market.
drills.hint: Movement toward a destination takes the goal preposition, not the static one.

drills.translation: She comes from Jakarta.
drills.hint: The city is where she started out, so this is the source preposition.

drills.translation: The cat is under the chair.
drills.hint: Position underneath something, stated with the static preposition before bawah.

drills.translation: Where are you from?
drills.hint: Origin: the preposition that marks the starting point someone comes out of.

drills.translation: I'll wait for you in front of the school.
drills.hint: Nobody is moving, so the static at/in/on preposition pairs with depan.

drills.translation: The children are not allowed into the kitchen.
drills.hint: Motion into a place: the goal preposition follows the verb of entering.

points.title: Aspect markers: sedang, masih, pernah, baru
points.function: Say in-progress, still, ever, and just-now
points.explanation: Indonesian marks aspect with free words before the verb, never on the verb: sedang/lagi 'in the middle of', masih 'still', sudah 'already', belum 'not yet', pernah 'have ever', baru (saja) 'just now', akan 'will'. belum and pernah are the pair English learners miss: Saya belum makan 'I haven't eaten YET' — the meal is still expected.

drills.translation: I'm eating right now.
drills.hint: In progress as you speak: the standard marker that goes before the verb, not the colloquial lagi.

drills.translation: She still lives here.
drills.hint: The situation began earlier and has not stopped, and one word before the verb says so.

drills.translation: Have you ever been to Bali?
drills.hint: Asking about experience at any point in a life, not about one particular time.

drills.translation: I've just arrived.
drills.hint: A moment ago, very recently; the marker pairs with saja here.

drills.translation: I have never eaten durian.
drills.hint: Never so far in a lifetime: after belum comes the marker of experience.

drills.sentence: Maaf, saya tidak bisa bicara sekarang, saya {{answer}} rapat.
drills.translation: Sorry, I can't talk right now, I'm in a meeting.
drills.hint: In the middle of something at this very moment, which is why the call has to wait.

drills.translation: Are you still hungry, or are you full now?
drills.hint: Asking whether the state carries on, set against sudah in the same question.

points.title: The -kan suffix: causative and benefactive
points.function: Make someone do it, or do it for someone
points.explanation: -kan does two jobs. Causative: besar 'big' → membesarkan 'enlarge'; jatuh 'fall' → menjatuhkan 'drop'. Benefactive: membeli 'buy' → membelikan 'buy FOR someone' (Saya membelikan dia buku). It also makes an intransitive verb take an object: duduk 'sit' → mendudukkan 'seat someone'.

drills.translation: I bought my sibling a book.
drills.hint: beli + meN- + -kan — for someone

drills.translation: He dropped the glass.
drills.hint: jatuh + -kan — made it fall

drills.translation: Please open the door (for me).
drills.hint: buka + -kan — imperative, benefactive

drills.translation: They grew that company.
drills.hint: besar + -kan — causative

drills.translation: Could you get me a glass of water?
drills.hint: From ambil 'to fetch'; before a vowel the active nasal is the velar one, and the benefactive ending marks the water as fetched for another person.

drills.sentence: Perawat itu {{answer}} nenek di kursi roda.
drills.translation: The nurse sat grandma down in the wheelchair.
drills.hint: From duduk 'to sit'; the causative suffix makes it something done TO a person, and the root's final k doubles in front of it.

points.title: The -i suffix: location and repetition
points.function: Point the verb at a place, or at repeated action
points.explanation: -i marks the object as a LOCATION or surface (duduk 'sit' → menduduki 'occupy'; datang 'come' → mendatangi 'go to'), or makes the action repeated/plural (pukul 'hit' → memukuli 'beat repeatedly'). Compare with -kan: menanamkan pohon 'plant a tree (cause it to be planted)' vs menanami kebun 'plant the garden (cover it)'.

drills.translation: The army occupied the city.
drills.hint: duduk + -i — the city is the LOCATION

drills.translation: He came to our house yesterday.
drills.hint: datang + -i — goal as object

drills.translation: The farmer planted the field with rice.
drills.hint: tanam + -i — covers the field

drills.translation: Don't beat that child.
drills.hint: pukul + -i — repeated action

drills.translation: Have you contacted that doctor yet?
drills.hint: From hubung 'to connect'; the location suffix aims the verb straight at the doctor, so no preposition is needed.

drills.translation: We climbed the stairs up to the fifth floor.
drills.hint: From naik 'to go up'; the suffix makes the stairs the direct object of the climb instead of a place phrase.

points.title: peN- nouns: the doer
points.function: Name the person or thing that does it
points.explanation: peN- takes the same nasal changes as meN- and names the agent or instrument: baca → pembaca 'reader', tulis → penulis 'writer', kerja → pekerja 'worker', dingin → pendingin 'cooler'. Learn it beside meN- — same nasal rule, so one pattern buys you both.

drills.translation: She is a famous writer.
drills.hint: tulis + peN- → pen-, t drops

drills.translation: This book has many readers.
drills.hint: baca + peN- → pem-

drills.translation: The workers go home at five.
drills.hint: kerja + peN- → pe-

drills.translation: He is a teacher of Indonesian.
drills.hint: ajar + peN- → peng-

drills.sentence: Di kamar ini tidak ada {{answer}} ruangan.
drills.translation: There is no air conditioner in this room.
drills.hint: From dingin 'cold'; the doer prefix names instruments as well as people, and before d its nasal is the dental one.

drills.translation: Who is the singer of this song?
drills.hint: From nyanyi 'to sing'; the doer prefix merges with the root's own nasal at the joint.

drills.translation: I asked the seller about the price.
drills.hint: From jual 'to sell'; the doer prefix takes the same nasal before j that the active verb prefix takes.

points.title: ke-...-an and per-...-an nouns
points.function: Build abstract nouns from anything
points.explanation: ke-...-an makes abstractions and states: bebas 'free' → kebebasan 'freedom'; ada → keadaan 'situation'. It also makes accidental/adversative verbs: hujan → kehujanan 'get caught in the rain'. per-...-an names the process or the place: usaha → perusahaan 'company'; tani → pertanian 'agriculture'. These two build most of the abstract vocabulary in a newspaper.

drills.translation: They fought for freedom.
drills.hint: bebas + ke-...-an

drills.translation: He works at a big company.
drills.hint: usaha + per-...-an

drills.translation: I got caught in the rain on the way.
drills.hint: hujan + ke-...-an — adversative

drills.translation: The economic situation is improving.
drills.hint: ada + ke-...-an

drills.sentence: Saya meminjam buku ini dari {{answer}} kota.
drills.translation: I borrowed this book from the city library.
drills.hint: From pustaka 'books, literature'; the circumfix that names a place or an institution, the same one behind the word for a company.

drills.translation: How is your mother's health now?
drills.hint: From sehat 'healthy'; the circumfix that turns a quality into the abstract state of having it.

drills.sentence: Saya belum mendapat {{answer}} untuk berbicara dengan dia.
drills.translation: I haven't had a chance to talk with him yet.
drills.hint: From sempat 'to have time for'; the same abstract-noun circumfix, naming what you are given rather than what you do.

points.title: yang: the all-purpose relativiser
points.function: Join a description to a noun
points.explanation: yang links a noun to whatever describes it — a clause, an adjective, a whole phrase: orang yang tinggi 'the person who is tall', buku yang saya baca 'the book that I read'. It also nominalises on its own: yang merah 'the red one'. It is the single most frequent grammatical word in Indonesian prose.

drills.translation: That tall person is my teacher.
drills.hint: The relativiser hooks the adjective onto the noun in front of it, giving 'the person who is tall'.

drills.translation: The book I read yesterday is lost.
drills.hint: Here it introduces a whole clause describing the book. English can leave this word out ('the book I read'); Indonesian keeps it.

drills.translation: I want the red one.
drills.hint: With no noun in front of it, the relativiser stands on its own and means 'the one that is...'.

drills.translation: This is the house my father built.
drills.hint: The same word again, this time in front of a di- passive clause: 'the house that was built by my father'.

drills.sentence: Mana {{answer}} lebih murah, ini atau itu?
drills.translation: Which one is cheaper, this or that?
drills.hint: A choice question needs the relativiser after mana: 'which is the one that is cheaper'.

drills.sentence: Dia siswa {{answer}} paling rajin di kelas.
drills.translation: He is the most diligent student in the class.
drills.hint: The linker goes between the noun and a superlative description built with paling.

drills.sentence: Rumah {{answer}} di sebelah kantor pos itu sudah dijual.
drills.translation: The house next to the post office has already been sold.
drills.hint: The same relativiser can head a bare place phrase, not only a clause: 'the house that is beside...'.

points.title: Passive type 1 and type 2
points.function: Choose the right passive for the person doing it
points.explanation: Type 1 is di- + verb, for third persons: Buku itu dibaca oleh Ali. Type 2 drops di- and puts a FIRST or SECOND person pronoun straight before the bare root: Buku itu saya baca 'The book was read by me', Buku itu kamu baca. Saying *dibaca oleh saya is understood but marked — native speakers use type 2.

drills.translation: I read that letter yesterday.
drills.hint: type 2 — pronoun + bare root

drills.translation: This book was read by Ali.
drills.hint: type 1 — di- for a third person

drills.translation: You've eaten that rice.
drills.hint: Type 2 again: after the aspect marker the actor's pronoun sits straight before the bare root. One listener, addressed informally - the everyday counterpart of the polite Anda, not the plural kalian.

drills.translation: That work was finished by them.
drills.hint: type 1

drills.translation: We have to solve this problem together.
drills.hint: Type 2: the actor's pronoun goes after the modal and directly before the bare root. Use the 'we' that includes the listener.

drills.translation: This cake was made by my grandmother.
drills.hint: Type 1 on buat 'to make'. Oleh may be left out when the actor follows the verb immediately.

points.title: Purpose: untuk, supaya, agar
points.function: Say what something is for
points.explanation: untuk + verb/noun is 'for, in order to' (Saya datang untuk belajar). supaya and agar introduce a purpose CLAUSE with its own subject (Saya belajar supaya bisa lulus 'so that I can pass'); agar is the more formal of the two. biar is the colloquial equivalent.

drills.translation: I came to study.
drills.hint: the purpose preposition that sits straight in front of a bare verb — no new subject can follow it

drills.sentence: Dia bekerja keras {{answer}} anaknya bisa sekolah.
drills.translation: He works hard so his child can study.
drills.hint: the everyday conjunction that opens a full purpose clause with its own subject

drills.translation: Please speak slowly so that I understand.
drills.hint: the formal-register partner of the everyday purpose conjunction — the one you meet in writing and in polite requests

drills.translation: This is for you.
drills.hint: the purpose preposition, this time before a person: it marks who a thing is meant for

drills.translation: What are you learning Indonesian for?
drills.hint: the purpose preposition opening a 'what for?' question — the same word that precedes a bare verb

drills.sentence: Ibu menyiapkan sarapan lebih pagi {{answer}} kami tidak terlambat.
drills.translation: Mum made breakfast earlier so that we wouldn't be late.
drills.hint: everyday conjunction, spoken register: the clause after it has a different subject from the main clause, and it is negative

drills.sentence: Sekolah menambah jam belajar {{answer}} siswa siap menghadapi ujian.
drills.translation: The school added study hours so that the students are ready to face the exam.
drills.hint: the written-register purpose conjunction a school announcement would choose over the everyday one

points.title: Conditionals: kalau, jika, bila
points.function: Say if
points.explanation: kalau is the everyday 'if' and also 'as for' (Kalau saya, saya setuju). jika and bila are the written equivalents; apabila is stiffer still. Indonesian marks no unreality on the verb — seandainya/andaikan carry the counterfactual sense that English puts into 'if I were'.

drills.translation: If it rains, I won't go.
drills.hint: the everyday spoken 'if' — the one you would say to a friend, not the written or legal ones

drills.translation: If you agree, please sign.
drills.hint: the formal written 'if' that goes with Anda and a signature line; plainer than the bureaucratic one, and it never doubles as 'when'

drills.sentence: {{answer}} saya kaya, saya akan keliling dunia.
drills.translation: If I were rich, I'd travel the world.
drills.hint: the verb carries no unreality in Indonesian, so the conjunction must — the one that flags the condition as contrary to fact

drills.translation: If necessary, contact me.
drills.hint: the short written conditional that also reads as 'when', standard in instructions and notices

drills.sentence: Saya tidak akan pergi {{answer}} kamu tidak ikut.
drills.translation: I won't go if you don't come along.
drills.hint: the same everyday conditional, this time joining the two clauses in the middle rather than opening the sentence

drills.translation: As for me, that price is too expensive.
drills.hint: no condition here at all: the everyday conditional word doing its other job, fronting a topic — 'speaking for myself'

drills.sentence: {{answer}} kemarin tidak hujan, kami pasti sudah berangkat.
drills.translation: If it hadn't rained yesterday, we would certainly have left.
drills.hint: the rain did fall, so the plain everyday word would be too weak — use the conjunction that marks a condition as contrary to fact

points.title: The se- prefix: one, same, whole
points.function: Say same-as, one, and all-of
points.explanation: se- means 'one' (sebuah, seorang, sehari 'one day'), 'same' (sekelas 'in the same class', sekantor 'in the same office'), 'as … as' on adjectives (sebesar 'as big as'), and 'the whole of' (seluruh dunia, sekeluarga 'the whole family'). One prefix, four jobs — context separates them.

drills.translation: We're in the same class at university.
drills.hint: se- — same

drills.translation: His house is as big as a palace.
drills.hint: se- + adjective — as … as

drills.translation: I waited one day.
drills.hint: se- — one

drills.translation: The whole family came.
drills.hint: se- — the whole of

drills.sentence: Bahasa Indonesia tidak {{answer}} yang kamu kira.
drills.translation: Indonesian isn't as hard as you think.
drills.hint: the equality prefix on sulit — 'as … as', negated here, with a whole clause as the yardstick

drills.sentence: Dia {{answer}} dengan saya, tetapi kami jarang bertemu.
drills.translation: He works in the same office as me, but we rarely run into each other.
drills.hint: kantor takes the 'same' prefix — one word does the work of 'in the same office as'

drills.sentence: Ada {{answer}} tamu yang menunggu Anda di lobi.
drills.translation: There is a guest waiting for you in the lobby.
drills.hint: the 'one' prefix fused to the classifier for people — the ordinary way to introduce a single unnamed person

points.title: The ter- prefix: accidental, stative, capable
points.function: Say it happened by itself, or by accident
points.explanation: ter- is the prefix with no English single equivalent. Accidental: Saya terjatuh 'I fell (unintentionally)'; Dompet saya tertinggal 'I left my wallet behind'. Stative result: pintu terbuka 'the door is (standing) open' — a state, versus dibuka 'was opened' — an event. Capability, usually negated: tidak terangkat 'can't be lifted'. And the superlative you already met: terbesar.

drills.translation: I fell on the stairs.
drills.hint: ter- — accidental, nobody's fault

drills.translation: I left my wallet at home.
drills.hint: ter- — unintended

drills.translation: That door has been open since morning.
drills.hint: ter- — a state, not an event

drills.translation: He couldn't lift that stone.
drills.hint: ter- — capability, negated

drills.sentence: Maaf, pesan itu {{answer}} ke grup yang salah.
drills.translation: Sorry, that message went to the wrong group.
drills.hint: kirim + ter- — it went off by accident, not because anyone decided to

drills.sentence: Aturan itu {{answer}} jelas di halaman pertama.
drills.translation: That rule is set out clearly on the first page.
drills.hint: tulis + ter- — the standing state of the page, not the act someone performed, which would take di-

drills.translation: Can my voice be heard from the back?
drills.hint: dengar + ter- — the question is whether it is possible at all, not whether anyone is doing it

points.title: memper-: causatives on adjectives
points.function: Make something more X
points.explanation: memper- + adjective means 'make more X': besar → memperbesar 'enlarge', baik → memperbaiki 'repair, improve', luas → memperluas 'widen'. Note memperbaiki takes -i as well. With nouns it means 'treat as': memperbudak 'enslave', memperistri 'take as a wife'. Formal registers reach for it constantly.

drills.translation: We'll enlarge this office.
drills.hint: memper- + besar

drills.translation: He is repairing his car.
drills.hint: memper- + baik + -i

drills.translation: The government widened that road.
drills.hint: memper- + luas

drills.translation: They strengthened relations between the two countries.
drills.hint: memper- + erat

drills.sentence: Saya harus {{answer}} paspor saya bulan depan.
drills.translation: I have to renew my passport next month.
drills.hint: panjang + memper- — making something run longer, here a document's validity

drills.translation: Can we speed up this process?
drills.hint: cepat + memper- — make it go faster; asked as a question about the whole process

drills.sentence: Undang-undang melarang siapa pun {{answer}} orang lain.
drills.translation: The law forbids anyone from enslaving another person.
drills.hint: budak + memper- — the noun sense of the prefix: treat a person AS one

points.title: Reduplication beyond the plural
points.function: Use doubling for casualness, variety, and reciprocity
points.explanation: Doubling isn't only plural. jalan-jalan 'go for a stroll' (casual, aimless), buah-buahan 'fruits of various kinds', sesekali 'now and then', tolong-menolong 'help one another', mata-mata 'spy' (lexicalised). The plural sense is only one reading, and it's dropped whenever a number or classifier already marks it: tiga buku, never *tiga buku-buku.

drills.translation: We strolled on the beach yesterday.
drills.hint: reduplication — casual activity

drills.translation: He sells all sorts of fruit at the market.
drills.hint: -an reduplication — variety

drills.translation: They help one another in hard times.
drills.hint: reduplication — reciprocal

drills.translation: I go there now and then.
drills.hint: se- + reduplication — occasionally

drills.sentence: Saya sudah membaca dua {{answer}} minggu ini.
drills.translation: I have already read two books this week.
drills.hint: the numeral is already doing the counting, so the noun must NOT be doubled — leave it in its plain form

drills.translation: Eat slowly, there is still plenty of time.
drills.hint: doubling an adjective here says HOW the action is done, not how many — join the two halves with a hyphen

drills.sentence: Dia ditangkap karena diduga menjadi {{answer}} asing.
drills.translation: He was arrested on suspicion of being a foreign spy.
drills.hint: a doubled body-part noun frozen into a job title — the halves no longer add up to two of anything

points.title: Reported speech with bahwa
points.function: Report what someone said or thought
points.explanation: bahwa introduces a reported clause: Dia bilang bahwa dia sakit. Indonesian has NO tense shift — the reported verb keeps whatever marker it had. bahwa is often dropped in speech (Dia bilang dia sakit) but kept in writing. Use kata/bilang for 'say' informally and mengatakan/menyatakan formally.

drills.translation: He said that he would come.
drills.hint: the connector that opens a reported clause after a verb of saying — kept in writing, commonly dropped in speech

drills.translation: I think that this is wrong.
drills.hint: the same reported-clause connector, here after a verb of thinking rather than of speaking

drills.translation: They said it was already finished.
drills.hint: the everyday spoken verb for 'say', filling the verb slot right after the subject — not the one a news report would use

drills.translation: The minister stated that prices would fall.
drills.hint: the most formal reporting verb, built on the root for 'evident' rather than the neutral one from 'word' — what ministers do at a podium

drills.translation: The doctor says I have to rest a lot.
drills.hint: informal reporting that opens the sentence with the bare noun for 'a saying', the speaker named straight after it — not the preposition menurut

drills.sentence: Dia bertanya {{answer}} saya bisa datang besok.
drills.translation: He asked whether I could come tomorrow.
drills.hint: a reported yes/no question takes the formal question marker, not the connector used for reported statements

points.title: Discourse particles: -lah, -kah, -pun
points.function: Add emphasis, question force, and 'even'
points.explanation: -lah softens an imperative or marks the focused word (Silakanlah masuk; Dialah yang salah 'HE is the one at fault'). -kah marks a yes/no question in formal or written style (Benarkah? 'Is that so?'). -pun means 'even, too' (Saya pun tidak tahu 'Even I don't know'). None translates directly; all three change the temperature of a sentence.

drills.translation: HE is the one responsible.
drills.hint: the focus clitic glued to the pronoun, throwing the weight of the sentence onto it — 'HE, and nobody else'

drills.translation: Is that news true?
drills.hint: the formal question clitic, attached to the word being questioned — it turns a written statement into a yes/no question

drills.translation: Even I don't know.
drills.hint: the 'even' particle after the subject, conceding that the speaker is no exception either

drills.translation: Please, do sit down.
drills.hint: the softening particle on the invitation verb — it makes an offer warm rather than commanding

drills.translation: Who was it that sent this letter?
drills.hint: the formal question clitic again, here fused to the question word itself, which makes the asking weightier

drills.translation: My younger sibling wants to come too.
drills.hint: the 'too, as well' particle standing after the subject — outside a few frozen conjunctions it is written as its own word, not glued on

drills.translation: Let us begin this meeting.
drills.hint: glued to mari, this particle turns 'come on' into a formal 'let us' at the head of the sentence

points.title: Formal connectors
points.function: Write the way a newspaper writes
points.explanation: Written Indonesian runs on connectors that rarely appear in speech: sehingga 'so that, with the result that', meskipun/walaupun 'although', namun 'however', oleh karena itu 'therefore', sedangkan 'whereas', selain itu 'besides that'. Learning ten of these is the fastest single step from conversational to readable.

drills.translation: It rained hard, so the road flooded.
drills.hint: the one-word connector that hangs the result on the clause before it, mid-sentence after the comma — written style

drills.translation: Although tired, he kept working.
drills.hint: 'although' at the head of the sentence, before the comma — the concessive that begins with m-

drills.translation: Prices rose. However, sales stayed good.
drills.hint: the formal sentence-opening 'however', set off by its own comma — where a joined clause would take tetapi

drills.translation: He is diligent, whereas his brother is lazy.
drills.hint: sets two people side by side in contrast — 'whereas', a plain opposition rather than a concession

drills.sentence: Anggaran belum cair. {{answer}}, proyek itu belum bisa dimulai.
drills.translation: The budget has not been disbursed. Therefore, the project cannot be started yet.
drills.hint: three words opening a new sentence to state the consequence — the formal counterpart of spoken jadi

drills.sentence: {{answer}}, apa lagi yang harus kita siapkan?
drills.translation: Apart from that, what else do we have to prepare?
drills.hint: two words that set aside what has already been covered and add a further item, opening the question

drills.sentence: Semua orang setuju, {{answer}} yang biasanya paling kritis.
drills.translation: Everyone agreed, even the ones who are usually the most critical.
drills.hint: pushes the claim one step further to the least expected case — 'even', mid-sentence after the comma

points.title: Agentless passives and oleh
points.function: Leave the doer out, or name it
points.explanation: The di- passive most often has NO agent at all — Rumah itu dijual 'The house is for sale/was sold' — and that is the neutral way to say it. When you do name the agent, oleh introduces it, and oleh itself is frequently dropped before a noun: dibaca (oleh) Ali. Indonesian reaches for the agentless passive where English would use an impersonal 'you' or 'they'.

drills.translation: That house was sold last year.
drills.hint: agentless di- passive

drills.translation: This problem must be resolved.
drills.hint: agentless, after a modal

drills.translation: That book was written by a doctor.
drills.hint: the preposition that names the doer of a passive — 'by', and freely dropped before a plain noun

drills.translation: Indonesian is used throughout the country.
drills.hint: agentless — the natural choice

drills.translation: When was this house built?
drills.hint: di- passive of the verb for building — a question about the date, with no builder named at all

drills.translation: Those dishes have not been washed since this morning.
drills.hint: di- passive of the verb for washing, negated with belum — nobody is named as the washer

drills.translation: Here rice is eaten by hand.
drills.hint: where English reaches for an impersonal 'you eat it', Indonesian turns the verb passive with di- and names nobody

points.title: Register: baku, colloquial, and Jakarta speech
points.function: Move between the written standard and how people talk
points.explanation: Bahasa baku (the standard) and everyday Jakarta speech differ enough to feel like two languages. saya/anda become gue/lu; the -kan suffix becomes -in (bikinin for membuatkan); meN- is often dropped entirely (Dia beli buku, not membeli); tidak becomes nggak/gak; sudah becomes udah. Textbooks teach only the first column, so learners understand the news and miss the conversation.

drills.translation: I don't know.
drills.hint: the Jakarta first-person pronoun that replaces saya among friends — the spelling ending in -e, not its -a twin

drills.translation: Make me a coffee.
drills.hint: -in for -kan, colloquial

drills.translation: Seems he's already gone.
drills.hint: the colloquial hedge for 'it seems', where baku prose would write sepertinya

drills.translation: Where are you going?
drills.hint: the two-letter Jakarta second-person pronoun that replaces anda between friends — the spelling with -u, not its -o twin

drills.translation: Have you eaten yet?
drills.hint: Jakarta speech clips the first letter off the baku completive marker; here it opens the question

drills.translation: He bought a new shirt yesterday.
drills.hint: colloquial speech drops the meN- prefix entirely — give the bare root of the verb for buying

drills.translation: The coffee here is really good!
drills.hint: the Jakarta intensifier that follows the adjective, standing in for baku sekali

points.title: Nominalisation in formal prose
points.function: Read the noun-heavy style of official Indonesian
points.explanation: Formal Indonesian turns verbs into nouns far more than English: instead of 'the government decided', pengambilan keputusan oleh pemerintah 'the taking of the decision by the government'. peN-...-an names the process (pembangunan 'development', penelitian 'research'); ke-...-an names the state (kebijakan 'policy', keamanan 'security'). Official prose stacks these, and unpacking them is the C1 reading skill.

drills.translation: Construction of the toll road is underway.
drills.hint: peN-...-an — the process

drills.translation: Government policy has changed.
drills.hint: ke-...-an — the state/abstraction

drills.translation: She conducted research for two years.
drills.hint: peN-...-an from teliti

drills.translation: National security is a priority.
drills.hint: ke-...-an from aman

drills.translation: When will the election of the new chairman be held?
drills.hint: peN-...-an turns 'to choose' into the event itself — a p-initial root disappears into the nasal

drills.translation: The education budget was raised this year.
drills.hint: peN-...-an on the root for 'to educate' — a d-initial root keeps its d after the nasal

drills.translation: This test measures the students' language ability.
drills.hint: ke-...-an on the root for 'able' — the abstract quality, not a person and not a process

points.title: Affix pairs that shift meaning
points.function: Tell apart verbs that share a root
points.explanation: The same root under different affixes gives related but distinct verbs, and no rule predicts the gap. mengajar 'teach (as an activity)' / mengajarkan 'teach (a subject)' / mengajari 'teach (a person)'. mendengar 'hear' / mendengarkan 'listen to'. menanam 'plant (something)' / menanami 'plant (a place)' / menanamkan 'instil'. These have to be learned as vocabulary, not derived.

drills.translation: She teaches at the school.
drills.hint: No suffix on the verb at all. The unsuffixed meN- form is what you get when the subject taught simply follows the verb and no recipient is introduced with kepada: teaching as the work she does, not teaching aimed at particular people.

drills.translation: She teaches me Javanese.
drills.hint: The person receiving the lessons is the direct object, not the subject being taught; that is what puts the -i suffix on the verb.

drills.translation: I listen to music every night.
drills.hint: Attending to the sound on purpose rather than just catching it; the deliberate verb carries -kan over the plain perception form.

drills.translation: The teacher instils the value of honesty.
drills.hint: Planting in the figurative sense, a value into people: what is instilled stays the object, and the verb carries -kan.

drills.sentence: Apakah kamu tidak {{answer}} suara aneh tadi malam?
drills.translation: Didn't you hear a strange noise last night?
drills.hint: Sound that simply reached your ears, with no effort behind it: the bare meN- verb takes no suffix, unlike the one for attending on purpose.

drills.sentence: Ibu saya {{answer}} bahasa Inggris kepada anak-anak di desa itu.
drills.translation: My mother teaches English to the children in that village.
drills.hint: What is passed on is the subject matter, and the people receiving it are marked with kepada; that pairing calls for the -kan suffix rather than the plain verb.

points.title: Switching register inside one text
points.function: Change level mid-text the way Indonesians do
points.explanation: A single Indonesian text moves between registers on purpose: a news report quotes a minister in baku and a bystander in colloquial; a novel narrates in standard prose and writes dialogue in Jakarta speech. Fiction and journalism both depend on the reader hearing the switch. Producing it — knowing when to drop meN-, when to keep bahwa — is the last thing to arrive.

drills.translation: The minister stated that prices would be stable.
drills.hint: A minister quoted in a formal report keeps the complementiser that introduces the reported clause; ordinary speech would leave it out.

drills.translation: "Have you heard yet?" his friend asked.
drills.hint: Inside the quotation the friend drops all the way into Jakarta street slang, not merely informal standard: the second-person pronoun that pairs with gue, borrowed from Hokkien, rather than the neutral form a textbook teaches or the polite written one.

drills.translation: The government is taking a new step.
drills.hint: full meN- — narration stays formal

drills.translation: He said, "Just leave it."
drills.hint: Reported speech keeps the speaker's own register, so the perfective adverb turns up in its clipped colloquial shape rather than the standard written one.

drills.sentence: "Apakah {{answer}} sudah menerima surat resmi kami?" tanya petugas itu dengan sopan.
drills.translation: "Have you received our official letter?" the officer asked politely.
drills.hint: An official speaking on the record addresses the public with the polite written second-person pronoun, the one that keeps its capital letter mid-sentence; the Jakarta form belongs in the other quotations.

drills.sentence: "Gue udah {{answer}} sama dia kemarin," katanya kepada atasannya.
drills.translation: "I already talked to him yesterday," he told his boss.
drills.hint: Inside the quotation the register drops: the verb for speaking appears with the Jakarta nasal prefix on a colloquial root, not the ber- form the narration would use.

drills.sentence: "Kaget banget gue!" kata seorang warga. Gedung {{answer}} memang berada tepat di seberang rumahnya.
drills.translation: "I got such a shock!" said one resident. The building in question is indeed right across from his house.
drills.hint: The register climbs again once the quotation ends: in the reporter's own prose, something already named is picked out with the written-register demonstrative rather than the everyday pointing word.

points.title: Lexicalised affixation
points.function: Recognise affixed words that no longer mean what the parts mean
points.explanation: Many affixed words have drifted from their roots and must be read whole. mengerti 'understand' has no live root *erti for most speakers; kemarin 'yesterday' is not ke- + marin; pengaruh 'influence' looks like peN- + garuh but isn't; berhasil 'succeed' is not simply ber- + hasil 'result'. Trying to decompose these produces confident wrong guesses — which is exactly the C2 trap.

drills.translation: I don't understand what you mean.
drills.hint: Learned whole: the verb for grasping what someone means carries meN- over a root that no longer stands on its own.

drills.translation: That effort finally succeeded.
drills.hint: A ber- verb that has drifted from the noun beneath it; 'come off, work out' is not what the prefix plus that noun would predict, so it is stored as one item.

drills.translation: He has great influence here.
drills.hint: It wears what looks like the peN- prefix, but no root is left underneath: an ordinary noun for the sway a person holds, learned as a unit.

drills.translation: Yesterday I met him.
drills.hint: The word for the day before today only looks like ke- over a root; nothing is being derived, so the whole form is the vocabulary item.

drills.sentence: {{answer}} Anda, apakah harga tiket akan turun tahun depan?
drills.translation: In your opinion, will ticket prices come down next year?
drills.hint: It has the shape of an active meN- verb, but the word that introduces whose view this is works as a preposition and never takes an object suffix.

points.title: Journalistic style: fronting and ellipsis
points.function: Read headlines and dense reporting
points.explanation: Indonesian journalism fronts the affected thing, leans on the passive, and drops pronouns wherever the reader can recover them. Headlines strip further still — articles, di-, even verbs go: 'Harga BBM Naik' (Fuel Prices Rise), 'Tersangka Ditangkap' (Suspect Arrested). Reading fluently means restoring what has been left out.

drills.translation: The suspect was arrested by police last night.
drills.hint: passive, agent after

drills.translation: Fuel prices rose five percent.
drills.hint: bare root — headline style

drills.translation: The victim was rushed to the nearest hospital.
drills.hint: di- passive, agent omitted

drills.translation: The meeting was postponed until next week.
drills.hint: di- passive, agentless

drills.translation: President to visit Papua next week.
drills.hint: A headline throws out the verb of motion altogether and leaves only the simplest directional preposition in front of the destination.

drills.sentence: Data itu belum kami {{answer}} sampai kemarin sore.
drills.translation: We had not received the data as of yesterday afternoon.
drills.hint: With the affected thing fronted and the agent pronoun standing immediately in front of it, the passive verb appears as a bare root: no meN-, no di-.

drills.sentence: Puluhan rumah di kampung itu {{answer}} banjir sejak Selasa dini hari.
drills.translation: Dozens of houses in that village have been submerged by floodwater since early Tuesday morning.
drills.hint: Nobody did this on purpose, so reporting reaches for the resultative ter- prefix rather than di-, and the water that caused it follows with no oleh.
